title: Start with CPU memory.
lead: Follow the same values across the CPU and GPU boundary.
captions: Chapter Two starts with five floating-point values in a CPU tensor. Their storage is in system RAM. Each value uses four bytes in the chosen format.
We are following a discrete GPU with separate device memory. The names x CPU and x GPU help us track location; the names themselves do not move any values.

title: Copy the inputs to GPU memory.
lead: A new tensor keeps the same input values.
captions: Calling the tensor's to method with cuda as the destination requests a GPU copy. PyTorch arranges storage and copies five values: twenty bytes of tensor data.
The original CPU tensor still exists. The copy contains the same numbers in different storage; copying has not doubled them.

title: Calculate where the tensor lives.
lead: The result stays on the GPU.
captions: Multiply the GPU tensor by two. The result, y GPU, has its own GPU storage. The input x GPU keeps its original values.
This operation copies zero bytes between CPU and GPU. That does not mean zero memory activity: the calculation still reads inputs and writes outputs in GPU memory.

title: Request the result on the CPU.
lead: Copying back is a separate operation.
captions: Calling CPU on the result requests a CPU copy. The values two, four, six, eight and ten now also have storage in system RAM.
Twenty bytes cross back in this example. The GPU result remains on the GPU; PyTorch does not automatically move every calculation's result to the CPU.

title: Count transfers separately.
lead: Copy in, calculate, then copy out.
captions: Across this sequence, twenty bytes of tensor data go in, zero cross during multiplication, and twenty come back. That is forty bytes copied between devices.
These are payload counts for the chosen example. They exclude other traffic and overhead, and they do not tell us how long the operations take.

title: Keep related calculations together.
lead: A GPU result can feed another GPU calculation.
captions: If another calculation needs the GPU result, it can read it there. A CPU copy is needed when a CPU-side consumer needs the values.
Choosing where to keep values can avoid unnecessary round trips. Whether that improves an application's speed depends on its actual operations and measurements.

title: Pause: copy eight results.
lead: Eight inputs. Multiply by three on the GPU.
captions: Try eight values instead, each still using four bytes. The GPU has multiplied them by three. Now request a CPU copy of y GPU.
Which values appear in the CPU result, and how many bytes of tensor data cross back? Does this copy change the original CPU input? Pause and explain the storage locations.

title: A copy preserves the values.
lead: New storage, with the GPU result's numbers.
captions: The CPU result contains three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-one and twenty-four. Eight values at four bytes each means thirty-two bytes copied back.
The original CPU input is unchanged. Return to Chapter Two and trace which operation creates each destination tensor, separating copies from calculation and from timing claims.
